title: Gold Coast Customs
description: The great satire of the London season and the waste land of the west. It is a verse work of 1929 by Edith Sitwell; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Gold Coast Customs sets the cannibal feasts of the Gold Coast against the dinners of the London season, in the long chanted line of the drum and the jazz band, and carries the satire of the rich into the elegy of the civilisation that eats its own.

literary_form: Long poem (the satire of the London season)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line.
historical_context: London at the end of the 1920s, and the satire of the waste land. The record dates the work as composed between 1928 and 1929 and first published in 1929 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
literary_significance: Gold Coast Customs is Edith Sitwell's greatest poem before the war elegies: its drum, its jazz and its cannibal feast made the satire of the rich a poem of the waste land and gave English modernism its most sustained indictment of the pleasure economy.

title: A Place of One's Own

narrative_structure: A ghost novel in chapters, from the purchase of the house to the last night in the room. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.

title: The Man Who Lost Himself
